stem.text: Figure 3.1 shows a reaction scheme starting from 4-hydroxybutanoic acid.

stem.caption: Figure 3.1
stem.alt: Reaction scheme. At the top, the structure of 4-hydroxybutanoic acid, HO-CH2-CH2-CH2-COOH. Four arrows lead away from it: a double-headed equilibrium arrow labelled H+(aq) down to G, C4H6O2; a single arrow labelled H+(aq) down to H, (C4H6O2)n; a single arrow labelled excess PCl5 down to J; a single arrow labelled [O] down to butanedioic acid, HOOC(CH2)2COOH.

stem.text: Under acidic conditions, 4-hydroxybutanoic acid exists in equilibrium with compound G, C4H6O2, and water. G does not react with Na.
4-hydroxybutanoic acid can also react to form condensation polymer H, which has formula (C4H6O2)n.
Draw the structures of G and H. Show only one repeat unit of H.

points.text: G: 5-membered cyclic ester (γ-lactone) formed by intramolecular esterification; H: polyester repeat unit –O–(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>–C(=O)– with continuation bonds (dashes) at both ends

markScheme.note: The MS answer is drawn structures (G and H); shown as ms.figure.

figure.alt: Structural formulas of G (a 5-membered cyclic ester, gamma-lactone) and H (a polyester repeat unit, dash-O-(CH2)3-C(=O)-dash).

explanation.text: G is formed by intramolecular esterification: the –OH at C4 attacks the –COOH's carbonyl carbon within the same molecule, losing H2O and closing a 5-membered ring — a cyclic ester (lactone), γ-butyrolactone. Because G is a lactone, not a carboxylic acid, it has no acidic –OH/–COOH left to react with Na (unlike the starting acid). H is the condensation polymer formed when many molecules of 4-hydroxybutanoic acid join end-to-end: each molecule's –OH reacts with the next molecule's –COOH, losing H2O at each join, giving a repeating –O–(CH2)3–C(=O)– ester-linkage unit (one repeat unit drawn with continuation/dash bonds at both ends to show the chain continues).

reasoningChain: Recognise G forms by intramolecular reaction of the molecule's own –OH and –COOH, losing water and closing a ring.
Draw G as the resulting 5-membered cyclic ester (lactone).
Recognise H as an intermolecular condensation polymer: the same two functional groups react between different molecules instead of within one.
Draw H's repeat unit with the ester linkage and continuation bonds at both ends.

inferredMistakes.text: Omitting the continuation (dash) bonds at the ends of H's repeat unit, or adding an extra oxygen atom not present in the monomer, which the ER reports as common errors.
Not identifying G as an ester (missing the cyclic C(=O)–O linkage), which the ER reports many candidates failed to do.

stem.text: Construct an equation for the reaction of 4-hydroxybutanoic acid with an excess of PCl5, forming J.

markScheme.note: MS awards: organic product Cl(CH2)3COCl [1]; rest of equation [1].

explanation.text: PCl5 in excess converts both of 4-hydroxybutanoic acid's reactive groups: the –COOH is converted to an acyl chloride –COCl (the standard reaction of a carboxylic acid with PCl5, releasing POCl3 and HCl), and separately the –OH is converted to –Cl (the standard reaction of an alcohol with PCl5, releasing POCl3 and HCl again). With both groups converted, J is Cl(CH2)3COCl, and two full equivalents of PCl5 (one per group) are needed, giving two POCl3 and two HCl overall.

reasoningChain: Recall PCl5 converts a carboxylic acid –COOH to an acyl chloride –COCl.
Recall PCl5 also converts an alcohol –OH to –Cl.
Since 4-hydroxybutanoic acid has both groups and PCl5 is in excess, both react: 2 mol PCl5 needed, giving the dichloro/acyl-chloride product J, plus 2POCl3 + 2HCl.

inferredMistakes.text: Only converting the –COOH group to –COCl and leaving the –OH group unreacted, missing that excess PCl5 also chlorinates the hydroxyl group, which the ER reports as a common oversight.

stem.text: 4-hydroxybutanoic acid, HO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COOH, is a weak acid with K<sub>a</sub> = 1.91 × 10<sup>–5</sup> mol dm<sup>–3</sup> at 25 °C.
Calculate the pH of a 0.150 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> solution of HO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COOH at 25 °C.

explanation.text: For a weak acid, the approximation [H<sup>+</sup>] ≈ √(K<sub>a</sub>[HA]) is used (assuming dissociation is small, so the equilibrium concentration of undissociated acid ≈ the initial concentration, and [H<sup>+</sup>] ≈ [A<sup>–</sup>]). Substituting K<sub>a</sub> = 1.91×10<sup>–5</sup> and [HA] = 0.150 gives [H<sup>+</sup>] = 1.69×10<sup>–3</sup> mol dm<sup>–3</sup>, then pH = –log<sub>10</sub>[H<sup>+</sup>] = 2.77.

reasoningChain: Use [H+] = √(Ka × [HA]) for a weak monoprotic acid.
Substitute the given Ka and concentration.
Take –log10 of [H+] to find pH.

inferredMistakes.text: Calculating [H+] incorrectly (e.g. forgetting the square root, or using Ka×[HA] directly as pH), which the ER notes some candidates did, receiving the pH mark only by error carried forward.

stem.text: When HO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COOH(aq) is mixed with its conjugate base, a buffer solution can form.
Define buffer solution.

points.text: (a solution that) resists/opposes/minimises changes in pH
when small (amounts/volumes) of acid/H<sup>+</sup> and base/alkali/OH<sup>–</sup> are added to it

explanation.text: A buffer solution's defining property is that its pH stays nearly constant despite small additions of acid or base: added H<sup>+</sup> reacts with the conjugate base component, and added OH<sup>–</sup> reacts with the weak acid component, so the ratio of acid to conjugate base (and hence the pH) changes only slightly.

reasoningChain: State the solution resists/minimises pH change.
State this applies specifically when small amounts of acid or base are added.

stem.text: State the structural formula of the conjugate base of HO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COOH.

explanation.text: A conjugate base is what remains after an acid donates (loses) a proton, H<sup>+</sup>. HO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COOH loses the acidic H from –COOH (not the alcohol –OH, which is not acidic enough to dissociate here), leaving the carboxylate anion HO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>–</sup>.

reasoningChain: Identify which H is lost: the acidic H of the –COOH group.
Remove that H and add a negative charge to the resulting O to write the conjugate base.

stem.text: A student makes a buffer solution by reacting 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.150 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> HO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COOH with 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.200 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> NaOH(aq).
Calculate the pH of this buffer solution.
K<sub>a</sub> of HO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COOH = 1.91 × 10<sup>–5</sup> mol dm<sup>–3</sup> at 25 °C.

points.text: M1: moles of HA initially = (0.150 × 25.0/1000) OR 3.75×10<sup>–3</sup> mol AND moles of NaOH/moles of A<sup>–</sup> = (0.200 × 10.0/1000) OR 2.00×10<sup>–3</sup> mol
M2: remaining moles of HA = 3.75×10<sup>–3</sup> – 2.00×10<sup>–3</sup> OR 1.75×10<sup>–3</sup> mol

explanation.text: NaOH neutralises some of the weak acid, converting it to its conjugate base: moles of HA initially = 0.150 × (25.0/1000) = 3.75×10<sup>–3</sup> mol; moles of NaOH added = 0.200 × (10.0/1000) = 2.00×10<sup>–3</sup> mol. Each mole of NaOH converts one mole of HA to A<sup>–</sup>, so after reaction: remaining HA = 3.75×10<sup>–3</sup> – 2.00×10<sup>–3</sup> = 1.75×10<sup>–3</sup> mol, and A<sup>–</sup> formed = 2.00×10<sup>–3</sup> mol (equal to the NaOH used, since NaOH is the limiting reagent and reacts 1:1). Using the buffer (Ka) expression K<sub>a</sub> = [H<sup>+</sup>][A<sup>–</sup>]/[HA], rearranged to [H<sup>+</sup>] = K<sub>a</sub>×[HA]/[A<sup>–</sup>] — the total volume (35.0 cm<sup>3</sup>) cancels since it is common to both [HA] and [A<sup>–</sup>], so the mole ratio can be used directly. [H<sup>+</sup>] = 1.91×10<sup>–5</sup> × (1.75×10<sup>–3</sup>/2.00×10<sup>–3</sup>) = 1.67×10<sup>–5</sup>, giving pH = 4.78.

reasoningChain: Calculate initial moles of weak acid HA and moles of NaOH added.
Subtract to find remaining moles of HA, and note moles of A⁻ formed equal moles of NaOH added (1:1 reaction).
Substitute the mole ratio of HA:A⁻ into [H+] = Ka[HA]/[A–] (volume cancels), then take –log10 to find pH.

inferredMistakes.text: Using the reversed ratio [A–]/[HA] instead of [HA]/[A–] in the Ka expression, giving pH 4.66, which the ER explicitly reports as a common error.
Using the initial moles of HA (3.75×10⁻³) rather than the remaining moles after reaction with NaOH (1.75×10⁻³), giving pH 4.45, which the ER explicitly reports.

stem.text: 4-hydroxybutanoic acid, HO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COOH, can be used to produce butanedioic acid, HOOC(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>COOH.
Suggest a suitable reagent and conditions for this reaction.

explanation.text: Converting the primary alcohol end (–CH<sub>2</sub>OH) of 4-hydroxybutanoic acid to a second carboxylic acid group requires full oxidation, which needs a strong oxidising agent — acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> or KMnO<sub>4</sub> — used in excess and with heating (reflux), the standard conditions for oxidising a primary alcohol all the way to a carboxylic acid (rather than stopping at the aldehyde).

reasoningChain: Identify that the –CH2OH end needs oxidising to –COOH.
Recall the reagent for full oxidation of a primary alcohol: acidified K2Cr2O7 or KMnO4, in excess, with heat/reflux.

inferredMistakes.text: Omitting 'heat' from the answer, or specifying alkaline conditions instead of acidic, which the ER reports as common errors.

stem.text: A student does an experiment to determine the partition coefficient, K<sub>pc</sub>, of butanedioic acid between the immiscible solvents ethoxyethane and water.
State what is meant by partition coefficient.

points.text: (the) ratio of the concentrations of a solute between two solvents at equilibrium

explanation.text: The partition coefficient is specifically a ratio of concentrations (not solubilities, and not amounts) of the same solute in two immiscible solvents, measured once the system has reached equilibrium (the solute is no longer net-transferring between the two layers).

reasoningChain: State it is a ratio of concentrations of the solute between two (immiscible) solvents, at equilibrium.

inferredMistakes.text: Defining it in terms of solubility rather than a ratio of concentrations, or omitting 'at equilibrium', which the ER reports as common gaps.

stem.text: The student adds butanedioic acid to a flask containing 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of ethoxyethane and 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of water. The mixture is shaken and left to separate into two layers.

items: 10.00 cm<sup>3</sup> of the ethoxyethane layer requires 7.50 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.100 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> NaOH(aq) for complete reaction.
10.00 cm<sup>3</sup> of the aqueous layer requires 11.10 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.500 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> NaOH(aq) for complete reaction.

stem.text: HOOC(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>COOH + 2NaOH → NaOOC(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>COONa + 2H<sub>2</sub>O
Calculate the concentration of butanedioic acid in each solvent.
Hence, determine the value of the partition coefficient, K<sub>pc</sub>, of butanedioic acid between ethoxyethane and water.

labels: concentration of butanedioic acid in ethoxyethane = ... mol dm<sup>–3</sup>
concentration of butanedioic acid in water = ... mol dm<sup>–3</sup>

points.text: M1: [acid(ether)] = 0.0375 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> AND [acid(aq)] = 0.2775 mol dm<sup>–3</sup>

explanation.text: The titration equation shows 2 mol NaOH neutralise 1 mol of the diprotic acid, so moles of acid = moles of NaOH ÷ 2. For the ether layer: moles NaOH = 0.00750 × 0.100 = 7.50×10<sup>–4</sup> mol, so moles acid = 3.75×10<sup>–4</sup> mol in 10.00 cm<sup>3</sup>, giving [acid(ether)] = 3.75×10<sup>–4</sup>/0.01000 = 0.0375 mol dm<sup>–3</sup>. For the aqueous layer: moles NaOH = 0.01110 × 0.500 = 5.55×10<sup>–3</sup> mol, so moles acid = 2.775×10<sup>–3</sup> mol in 10.00 cm<sup>3</sup>, giving [acid(aq)] = 0.2775 mol dm<sup>–3</sup>. The partition coefficient is then K<sub>pc</sub> = [acid(ether)]/[acid(aq)] = 0.0375/0.2775 = 0.135 (no units, as it's a ratio of like concentrations).

reasoningChain: For each layer, find moles of NaOH used in its titration, then halve (2:1 acid:NaOH ratio) to get moles of diprotic acid in that 10.00 cm³ sample.
Divide by the 10.00 cm³ volume (as dm³) to get each layer's concentration.
Divide [acid(ether)] by [acid(aq)] to find Kpc.

inferredMistakes.text: Dividing the moles of acid by the original 0.025 dm³ (25.0 cm³) flask volume instead of the 0.010 dm³ (10.00 cm³) sample actually titrated, which the ER reports as a common error.
